why_this_batch_matters: Most customers do not know the difference between closed string / cut string / open string / open riser and use the terms interchangeably.
The string type materially affects construction cost, joinery detail, baluster attachment, base-rail requirement, visual character, and whether the flight can be placed against a wall on one side.
The concrete-substructure case is often mistaken for a timber cut-string build because the visual language is similar.
Cut string and Open string are the SAME thing — one construction detail, two regional names.
Open riser is a SEPARATE concept from string type — you can have a closed-string open-riser staircase or a cut-string closed-riser staircase.

qa.q: What's the difference between cut string and closed string?
qa.a: Closed string is a straight-topped plank running alongside the flight; the treads and risers slot into routed grooves inside it and their ends are hidden. Cut string has a stepped top edge that follows each tread and riser; the treads sit on top and their ends are exposed. Both are perfectly valid — the choice is aesthetic and cost, not one being better than the other.

qa.q: Is `open string` a different thing to cut string?
qa.a: No — `open string` and `cut string` are two names for the same construction. UK joinery workshops use both terms interchangeably. Different from `open riser`, which is a separate concept referring to the vertical board between treads being omitted.

qa.q: Which style is more traditional?
qa.a: Both are traditional — Victorian houses used both, often on the same staircase (closed on the wall side, cut on the exposed outer side). What reads `traditional` to most people is the newel and baluster style rather than the string type. Turned spindles read traditional; slim metal balusters read contemporary — either can sit on either string type.

qa.q: Which is more expensive?
qa.a: Cut string is usually a bit more expensive to make and install because the joinery is more exposed — treads need finished returns on the visible side, and balusters typically dovetail into the treads rather than land into a base rail. Closed string hides more of the joinery inside the string and is quicker to produce.

qa.q: Can I have one side of each?
qa.a: Yes — a common configuration is a closed string on the wall side and a cut string on the exposed side. It's neither a compromise nor unusual — it's a real choice that can look correct in the right home.

entries.philip_annotation: Closed string on its own — no steps or risers, just the string showing the routed housings.

analysis.description: A single isolated oak closed-string board photographed against a transparent / removed background. The plank has a straight top edge and a straight bottom edge (parallel), and four routed housings are visible on the inner face — each housing is a diagonal groove for the underside of a tread, a shallow rising groove for the back of the riser, and small wedge pockets at the tread-riser junction. This is the definitive visual identifier of a closed string: routed grooves on the inside face, straight top edge.
analysis.purpose: Component-in-isolation reference so a customer can see what a closed string looks like before the treads and risers are fitted.

routed diagonal grooves for tread undersides
shallow angled grooves for riser backs
small wedge pockets at tread-riser junctions

qa.q: What are those grooves for?
qa.a: They're routed housings that receive the treads and risers. Each tread slides into a diagonal groove, each riser slides into a shallower angled groove, and a wooden wedge is driven from underneath into a small pocket to lock everything tight. It's how a closed string holds a staircase together without any visible fixings.

qa.q: Do both strings have these grooves?
qa.a: Yes — if both strings on a staircase are closed strings, both carry the same housing pattern on their inner face. If one string is cut string, that one has treads sitting on top instead of housings inside.

qa.q: How thick is a typical closed string?
qa.a: 38-45mm (1½–1¾ inch) for a domestic staircase in a hardwood species. Softwood strings for paint-grade builds can be slightly thicker to keep stiffness. Actual thickness is set by the joinery workshop for the span and load.

qa.q: Why can't I see the treads and risers?
qa.a: This is the string on its own — before the staircase is assembled. Once fitted, the treads and risers slot into these grooves and the string is what you see running diagonally alongside the flight. From the outside, the string face stays smooth — the treads are hidden inside it.

qa.q: How does the balustrade attach on a closed string?
qa.a: A base rail sits on top of the closed string and the balusters land into the base rail. On a cut string, balusters land directly into the treads instead — that's one of the practical differences between the two string types.

qa.q: How can I tell this is a closed string?
qa.a: The outer string is a smooth diagonal plank with a straight top edge — you can see the string face but you cannot see the tread ends coming through it. The balusters land into a base rail on top of the string rather than into the treads themselves. Those two features together are the tell.

qa.q: Why is there a base rail here?
qa.a: Because the string is closed. Balusters can't dovetail into the tread ends (the tread ends are hidden inside the string) so they land into a base rail that sits on top of the string. On a cut string the balusters land directly into the treads instead and no base rail is needed on the flight.

qa.q: Is the bottom step curved?
qa.a: No — the bottom step here is a boxed / closed-string configuration where the string wraps around the bottom step. Bullnose starting steps are one option; boxed bottom steps are another and are common on closed-string builds against a wall.

qa.q: Can I have this look in walnut or painted?
qa.a: Yes — closed string is a construction detail, not a finish. The same build works in oak, walnut, ash, painted softwood, or a stained finish. Balusters can be metal or turned wood in whatever style suits.

qa.q: Would this fit against a wall?
qa.a: Yes — the wall side would be another closed string, closed against the plaster. This is the most common domestic configuration in the UK: closed string on both sides, one side against a wall.

qa.q: Why are both sides cut string?
qa.a: Because this staircase is freestanding and both sides are visible. When both sides show, both string tops are cut to match the tread profile — it looks intentional and symmetric. If one side were against a wall you could go with any of several configurations; when both are open, double-side cut is a common choice.

qa.q: How can I tell this is cut string?
qa.a: The top edge of each stringer is stepped, following each tread and riser. The tread ends visibly project past the stringer face on both sides. And the balusters land into the treads (with a dovetail or dropped pin) rather than into a base rail on top of the string.

qa.q: Where do the balusters go on a cut string?
qa.a: Straight into the top of each tread — traditionally with a dovetail joint that gets covered by the tread return moulding on the outside, or with a dropped-in pin on more contemporary builds. Two balusters per tread is the common spacing.

qa.q: Do I need to see all the tread ends? They look busy.
qa.a: It's aesthetic. Cut-string tread ends give a decorative rhythm that some homes love and some find busy. If you prefer a quieter look, closed string with the tread ends hidden inside a smooth diagonal plank is the alternative.

qa.q: Can this go against a wall?
qa.a: Yes — the far string can simply meet the wall. There's a real example in image 05 of this same batch where a double-side cut-string flight sits against a wall on one side. No newel is needed at the wall-adjacent top corner because the string terminates against the wall.

qa.q: Can a double-side cut-string staircase go against a wall?
qa.a: Yes — this is a real example. The wall-adjacent string simply meets the wall and terminates there. You don't need a newel post at the wall-side top corner because the string is captured by the wall. Both stringers stay cut string throughout their length.

qa.q: Why isn't there a newel post at the top-far corner?
qa.a: Because the string terminates against the wall. A newel is needed where a string ends in free air (bottom of the flight, or top-of-flight corner in the open) but not where the string is captured against a wall. It's a real, correct configuration.

qa.q: What's a `square quarter landing`?
qa.a: A small square-shaped landing at the top of the flight where the staircase turns 90° onto the upper floor. It's the smallest form of landing — big enough to stand on and turn, no more. Common when floor-plan geometry is tight.

qa.q: Isn't a cut string usually only on the open side?
qa.a: That's the older configuration and the one many joiners default to (closed on wall side, cut on open side). But double-side cut is a perfectly valid choice — either because both sides are visible or, as here, because the aesthetic wants both sides to read as cut even where one side happens to sit against a wall.

qa.q: Would balusters ever land into the wall side here?
qa.a: No — the wall itself takes the role of the balustrade on that side. Balusters only rise on the open (non-wall) side of the flight and on the open faces of the landing.

qa.q: Is this the same as an open string staircase?
qa.a: No — this is an OPEN RISER staircase, which is a different thing. Open riser means the vertical board between treads has been omitted so you can see through. The strings here are still closed strings (smooth diagonal plank). The two words are often confused but they refer to different parts of the staircase.

qa.q: Is there a safety issue with open risers?
qa.a: There's a rule about gap size — a specified sphere shouldn't be able to pass through the gap between treads (typically 100mm in UK Approved Doc K). Modern open-riser builds meet this by keeping tread spacing close enough. Some families with very young children also fit temporary riser-fill panels and remove them later.

qa.q: Why go open riser?
qa.a: It makes the staircase feel lighter and lets more light through — useful in an open-plan setting or a narrow hallway that needs to feel airy. It also lets people see the space beyond the staircase, so smaller floor plans feel bigger.

qa.q: Can I have open riser + cut string together?
qa.a: Yes — the two are independent. You can have any combination: closed string + closed riser (most traditional), closed string + open riser (like this image), cut string + closed riser, or cut string + open riser (most contemporary and most open-feeling).

qa.q: Is open riser more expensive?
qa.a: Usually a bit less — there's no riser board to make and fit. The trade-off is that the tread underside is visible so it may need to be finished on both faces rather than one.

qa.q: Is this a cut string staircase?
qa.a: Visually yes — it reads as cut string with a stepped outer edge and exposed tread ends. Structurally no — there is no timber string board. The staircase is built on a concrete substructure (or a concealed steel spine) and clad in oak. The stepped edge you see is CLADDING, not a load-bearing string.

qa.q: Why does it matter what's underneath?
qa.a: It matters for anyone specifying, quoting or repairing the staircase. A timber cut-string staircase and a concrete-clad staircase with the same visual look are entirely different builds — different trades, different costs, different repair approaches. Two staircases can look identical from three metres away and be built completely differently.

qa.q: How can I tell?
qa.a: Usually by context. Concrete substructure is common in modern architect-designed extensions, new-builds and commercial spaces. If the staircase is inside a Victorian terraced house, it's likely timber. If it's in a modern minimalist build with polished-concrete floors, it's likely concrete. Sometimes the only way to know is by asking the original builder or opening up the underside.

qa.q: Is this cheaper than a timber cut string?
qa.a: Rarely — concrete substructure work is a separate specialist trade (steel-fixer + concrete pour + curing time + oak cladding after). Total cost is usually higher than an equivalent timber-string joinery build. But the aesthetic can justify it in the right architectural setting.

qa.q: What about the wall side — no wooden string at all?
qa.a: That's right. The treads and risers meet the plastered wall directly. The wall itself does the closing function that a wall string would provide on a timber build. It's uncommon in domestic timber joinery but normal on concrete builds.

qa.q: Why mix closed and cut on the same staircase?
qa.a: Aesthetics and practicality. The formal outer face reads well as a smooth closed string; on the wall side the stepped cut treatment gives a cleaner meeting between tread ends and plaster wall than trying to bury the treads inside a full wall string. It's a real design choice, not a compromise.

qa.q: Is this common?
qa.a: Less common than closed-both-sides or cut-both-sides, but a recognised configuration. Some joinery workshops offer it as a specific option, particularly on straight flights against a wall where the outer face wants to read formal but the wall side is easier to detail cut.

qa.q: Where do the balusters go here?
qa.a: Into the base rail on top of the closed outer string — same as any closed-string flight. The wall side doesn't need balusters because the wall itself does the job of the balustrade there.

qa.q: How can I check on my own staircase?
qa.a: Stand at the bottom of the flight and look up the outer face. If the string is smooth, it's closed on that side. Then look along the wall side of the flight — if the treads step up against the wall in visible steps, the wall string is cut. If the wall side is a smooth diagonal plank against the wall, the wall string is also closed.

qa.q: Does the price differ?
qa.a: Slightly — a cut wall string can be quicker to fit against an existing plaster wall than a full closed wall string that has to be housed against irregular plaster. Details vary by joinery workshop, but the difference is normally small compared to the overall build cost.

qa.q: What's a `nosing`?
qa.a: The projecting front edge of a stair tread — the bit that overhangs the riser. Nosing profile is the shape of that edge (rounded, square, bevelled, chamfered) and it's a separate design decision from string type or riser type.

qa.q: Which nosing is most traditional?
qa.a: Standard bullnose — a fully rounded front edge that projects past the riser. It's the classic Victorian and Edwardian domestic profile and reads warm and welcoming. Modern nosings tend to be squarer or slightly softened.

qa.q: Which is safest?
qa.a: All three meet UK building standards for a compliant nosing projection. Bullnose tends to be perceived as safer underfoot because the rounded edge is softer. Square-nose profiles need a good visual contrast against the riser to read well on a dim stair.

qa.q: Can I change the nosing profile on my existing staircase?
qa.a: Only by replacing the treads (or the tread caps in a refacing build). The nosing is machined into the front edge of the tread itself; you can't retro-fit a different profile onto an existing tread without machining it away.

qa.q: Does the nosing depend on the string type?
qa.a: No — the nosing is a tread detail. Any of these three profiles can appear on a closed-string, cut-string or concrete-substructure staircase. What changes with string type is how the tread END is finished (return moulding on a cut string vs hidden inside the string on a closed string).

entries.philip_annotation: Cut string tread side return — how it's finished.

analysis.description: Extreme close-up of the front-right corner of an oak stair tread showing the RETURN piece that finishes the exposed tread end on a cut-string build. The main tread top surface runs across the top-right of the frame. A separate return piece runs along the exposed side edge of the tread, glued and pinned in place with a mitered 45° corner at the front where it meets the tread nosing. The wood grain flows continuously through the mitered corner, giving the appearance of a solid wrapped-around block rather than a raw end-grain edge.
analysis.purpose: Shows the joinery detail that finishes the visible tread end on a cut string — a small return moulding wraps the tread end so no end-grain is exposed.
notable_features: separate return moulding piece running along tread end
mitered 45° corner where return meets front nosing
grain flows continuously across the mitre
hides end-grain that would otherwise show on cut-string exposed side
hallmark of quality cut-string joinery

qa.q: What is this piece for?
qa.a: It's a tread return — a small piece of matching timber glued and pinned to the exposed side of a cut-string tread. It hides the end-grain that would otherwise show, and it wraps the front nosing round the corner so the tread looks like a solid block from the outside. Only used on cut-string staircases (closed-string tread ends are already hidden inside the string).

qa.q: Is the mitered corner difficult to make?
qa.a: It's careful joinery work — the mitre has to be tight enough that the grain reads as continuous. A good joinery workshop does this every day; a rushed build might show a gap or misalignment at the corner. This is one of the details a customer can check when quality-inspecting a finished cut-string staircase.

qa.q: Can I have a tread return in a different timber?
qa.a: Some designs deliberately contrast — walnut tread with an oak return, for example — but the norm is matching timber and matching grain direction for a seamless appearance.

qa.q: What happens if there's no return?
qa.a: You'd see raw end-grain on the exposed side of every tread. It looks unfinished and it's how you can tell a cut-string staircase was value-engineered or built to a budget. On a quality cut-string build, every exposed tread end has a return.

qa.q: Is a return the same as a mitered floating tread?
qa.a: No — a return is a separate small piece added to the tread. A mitered floating tread (see image 12 of this batch) is a solid slab where the front and side are one continuous piece with a mitered corner — no separate return needed. Different construction, different look.

analysis.description: Extreme close-up of a heavy-thickness oak floating tread cantilevered from a plastered wall. The tread reads as a single solid oak block — roughly 55-65mm thick — with a MITERED 45° corner at the front-outer edge (where the exposed side face meets the front face). No bullnose profile — the arrises are square with a slight eased softening. The grain wraps around the mitre continuously, giving the appearance of one solid block of wood rather than a return-piece assembly. Left side of frame is a plastered wall.
analysis.purpose: Shows the alternative to a tread-return finish — a heavy-thickness solid-block tread where the front-outer corner is mitered so no end-grain shows and no separate return piece is needed. Common on contemporary architectural floating staircases.
notable_features: heavy-thickness solid oak block (approximately 55-65mm)
mitered 45° corner at front-outer edge
no separate return piece — one solid block wrapped by mitre
no bullnose — square arrises with slight eased softening
cantilevered from wall (typical mounting for this style)

qa.q: How is this different from a tread with a return?
qa.a: This is a solid heavy-thickness block — the front face and the exposed side face are one continuous piece wrapped by a mitred corner. On a return build (image 11) the tread is a standard thickness and a small return moulding is glued onto the side. Different construction, different look, different price. This is the architectural / floating-stair language.

qa.q: Why so thick?
qa.a: Thick treads are structural on floating staircases where the tread cantilevers from a wall or spine — the thickness gives the tread the stiffness to carry loads without needing an underlying string. Also visually: a chunky solid slab reads as premium and architectural. Common thicknesses are 55-80mm on floating builds vs 25-40mm on a conventional string-built tread.

qa.q: Why no bullnose?
qa.a: Bullnose is a traditional / Victorian language. Contemporary floating stairs typically use square-edged treads with only a very slight softening at the arris — the visual language is `chunky slab`, not `warm rounded step`. Both are valid; the choice signals which era of design you're aiming for.

qa.q: Does this need special installation?
qa.a: Yes — floating cantilevered treads need a robust fixing hidden inside the wall (a steel spine, an embedded plate, or wall-fixed brackets). It's a structural build, sized by an engineer rather than a joiner. Not a retrofit unless the wall behind is opened up.

qa.q: Can I have this look with a closed string?
qa.a: No — the heavy floating tread is inherently a stringless / concealed-support construction. If you want a closed-string staircase, the treads sit in string housings and won't be a heavy solid block. If you want the chunky-slab look, you'll need a floating build or a concrete substructure clad in solid timber.

qa.q: What are the three parts of a stair face called?
qa.a: Tread (the horizontal you walk on) · riser (the vertical between treads) · return (the finished edge on the exposed side of the tread). Return only exists on a cut-string or exposed-side build — if the tread is fully closed inside a string, you don't see the tread end so no return is needed.

qa.q: Is this a full new staircase or a refacing?
qa.a: This diagram is showing a refacing system — treads and risers installed over an existing staircase. The three components (tread, riser, return) exist on any staircase, but the diagram is marketing a specific over-cladding approach where you cover the old surface without replacing the structure.

qa.q: Can I have walnut treads with white risers on a new build?
qa.a: Yes — the two-tone (dark wood tread + white/painted riser) is a valid new-build choice as well as a refacing choice. It's a common contemporary palette for both approaches.

qa.q: Do all staircases have returns?
qa.a: No — only staircases with exposed tread ends need returns. A closed-string staircase where both sides are closed against walls has no exposed tread ends and no returns. Cut-string staircases with an open side always have returns on that side.

qa.q: What's the point of a return?
qa.a: Two jobs — hiding the end-grain of the tread so the exposed side looks like a solid finished piece rather than a cut edge, and protecting the tread corner from bumps and wear. Without a return the tread end would look unfinished and would chip more easily.

Dimensions are given in imperial (US units).
analysis.purpose: Component-dimensioning reference — teaches customers the standard tread-depth and riser-height ranges. IMPORTANT: dimensions are in imperial (US); the UK equivalents differ and are governed by Approved Document K (see doc reference).
notable_features: tread depth range 8¼-14 inches (approx 210-355mm)
riser height range 5-7⅞ inches (approx 127-200mm)
nosing detail zoom showing rounded projection
US-imperial units — UK equivalents differ under Approved Doc K
same walnut-and-white treatment as image 13

qa.q: What's a `tread depth`?
qa.a: How far your foot can rest on the walking surface, measured from the front of one step to the front of the next. In UK terms this is called the `going`. Typical domestic going in the UK is 220-260mm; the imperial range shown here (8¼-14 inches / 210-355mm) is US IRC guidance, so the UK domestic range is at the lower end of that.

qa.q: What's the UK equivalent?
qa.a: UK Approved Document K (domestic): max riser 220mm, min going 220mm, with 2R + G between 550 and 700mm, and max pitch 42°. Common domestic actuals are riser ~180-190mm, going ~230-250mm, which fall comfortably inside those limits.

qa.q: Does the tread depth affect comfort?
qa.a: Yes — a shallow going forces the foot to overhang the nosing and feels less secure going down. A generous going feels safer and more like walking on a level floor. The trade-off is total horizontal run — a deeper going needs a longer floor area.

qa.q: Why does the diagram say `tread height`?
qa.a: That label is a bit confusing — the dimension it points to is the vertical rise between treads (which is more usually called `riser height` or just `rise`). The UK term is `rise`; the US term is either `rise` or `riser height`; `tread height` is not a standard UK term.

qa.q: How is nosing projection measured?
qa.a: It's the horizontal distance the front of the tread projects past the face of the riser below. UK Approved Doc K typically requires 15-25mm of projection for domestic stairs, but you'll see anywhere from a flush 0mm (modern flush-riser look) up to about 35mm (traditional deep bullnose).

qa.q: What's a `stairway width`?
qa.a: The clear width of the flight — measured between the inside faces of the two strings (or between wall and outer string on a wall-flanked flight). UK Approved Doc K minimum for domestic is 800mm clear; comfortable modern builds are usually 900-1000mm.

qa.q: What's the `run`?
qa.a: The total horizontal length the staircase covers on the floor — from the front of the bottom step to the front of the top step. For a domestic 13-tread flight at 240mm going, the run is around 3 metres.

qa.q: Are these US values applicable in the UK?
qa.a: These values (7-3/4 max riser, 10 min tread) are US IRC (International Residential Code). UK Approved Doc K sets a different envelope — max riser 220mm, min going 220mm, and a joint rule that 2R+G is between 550 and 700mm. The US and UK envelopes overlap on `comfortable stair` proportions but the extreme edges differ.

qa.q: Can a stair be too wide?
qa.a: Structurally rare, but there's a psychological width above which stairs start to feel `grand` rather than domestic — around 1200mm and up. Most domestic staircases sit between 800 and 1000mm clear. Wider stairs cost more (longer treads, more baluster spacing, potentially two handrails).

qa.q: How do I calculate how much floor space a new staircase needs?
qa.a: Total run = number of treads × going. For a typical 13-tread domestic flight at 240mm going = 3.12m of horizontal floor space. Plus space at the top (landing) and at the bottom (approach). Getting this right early is critical — retrofitting a staircase into a smaller footprint often forces a compromise on pitch or tread depth.
